links.outcome: Reference quality and fabricated citations in LLM outputs on pediatric GI vignettes
links.effect: Significant intermodel differences in reference quality (p = 0.048); Claude had highest reference quality; qualitative analysis found a high frequency of fabricated citations.
links.quote: Qualitative analysis revealed critical pharmacological dosing errors, contextual blindness, temporal obsolescence, and a high frequency of fabricated citations.

links.outcome: Pharmacological dosing errors in LLM responses to pediatric GI vignettes
links.effect: Qualitative analysis revealed critical, reproducible pharmacological dosing errors despite perfect diagnostic accuracy (median 2.00).
links.quote: Qualitative analysis revealed critical pharmacological dosing errors, contextual blindness, temporal obsolescence, and a high frequency of fabricated citations.

links.outcome: Currency and accuracy of clinical knowledge in LLM outputs
links.effect: All three models achieved perfect diagnostic accuracy (median 2.00, IQR 2.00-2.00), but qualitative analysis found temporal obsolescence.
links.quote: Qualitative analysis revealed critical pharmacological dosing errors, contextual blindness, temporal obsolescence, and a high frequency of fabricated citations.

screen.reason: Empirical evaluation of three LLMs using fictional clinical vignettes in pediatric gastroenterology, assessing clinical reasoning and safety failure modes without testing a specific organizational deployment practice or guardrail.
